t.textos.lista-reyes.version: Sumerian composition known from some 20 manuscripts, from one of the Ur III period (c. 2100 BC) to Old Babylonian copies from Isin and Larsa (c. 1800 BC); the most complete is the Weld-Blundell prism (WB 444, Ashmolean Museum)
t.textos.lista-reyes.estructura.0.sinops: Kingship descends from heaven to Eridu. Eight kings in five cities (Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar, Shuruppak) rule for a total of 241,200 years. Then comes the flood. This section is missing from some manuscripts and is probably an addition.
t.textos.lista-reyes.estructura.1.seccio: First dynasty of Kish and Uruk I (lines 40–133)
t.textos.lista-reyes.estructura.1.sinops: After the flood, kingship descends again from heaven to Kish, with reigns of hundreds of years; among the kings are Etana, "the shepherd who went up to heaven", and Enmebaragesi. It passes to Eanna (Uruk), with Meskiaggasher, Enmerkar, Lugalbanda, Dumuzi the fisherman and Gilgamesh (126 years).
t.textos.lista-reyes.estructura.2.sinops: Kingship passes in succession among Ur, Awan, Kish, Hamazi, Uruk, Adab, Mari, Kish (with Queen Kug-Bau), Akshak, Akkad (Sargon, Naram-Sin), the Gutian period, Uruk and Ur III. The reigns gradually become of human length.
t.textos.lista-reyes.estructura.3.sinops: The list ends with the dynasty of Isin (in some copies, with Larsa) and a total that adds up all the dynasties. The dynasty of Lagash, known from inscriptions, is absent: it appears in a separate, parodic "Lagash King List".
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.0.texto: "After kingship had descended from heaven, kingship was in Eridu". Paraphrase of the rest: in Eridu, Alulim became king and ruled for 28,800 years; Alalgar ruled for 36,000 years. Then Eridu fell and kingship was taken to Bad-tibira, where En-men-lu-ana (43,200 years), En-men-gal-ana (28,800) and Dumuzi the shepherd (36,000) ruled. Then came Larak (En-sipad-zid-ana, 28,800), Sippar (En-men-dur-ana, 21,000) and Shuruppak (Ubara-Tutu, 18,600). "In five cities, eight kings ruled for 241,200 years. Then the flood swept over everything".
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.0.fuente: Short quotation translated into Spanish from ETCSL 2.1.1 (Black et al.), line 1, and here into English from the Spanish; the rest, a faithful paraphrase with the figures of the WB 444 prism
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.0.nota_acad: The figures are in the sexagesimal system and are multiples of 3,600 (the sar) and 600: 28,800 is 8 sar, 36,000 is 10 sar. They vary from one manuscript to another, and some give other kings (for example, Ziusudra as the tenth). The list is an ideological text, probably composed in the Ur III period and reworked at Isin: it maintains that in Sumer there was only one legitimate kingship, which passed from city to city, when in reality many dynasties were contemporary. Berossus (3rd century BC) gives a Greek version with ten antediluvian kings and 120 sar (432,000 years). P. Steinkeller published the Ur III manuscript in 2003.
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.0.lectura_a: Sitchin interprets the reigns in multiples of 3,600 years as "Nibiru years": each sar would be one orbit of the planet, and the antediluvian kings would be Anunnaki commanders who ruled the Earth for 120 sar (432,000 years) before the flood.

The sar is a number (3,600 = 60 × 60), not an astronomical unit of time; in the list itself there are figures that are not multiples of 3,600 (21,000, 18,600, 43,200 are multiples of 600). The reigns decrease progressively down to human lengths, a device common in mythical genealogies such as that of Genesis 5. The total varies by manuscript (241,200 in WB 444, other figures in others), and the 120 sar come from Berossus, two thousand years later.
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.1.ref: Lines 40–133 (Kish and Uruk) and the entry for Kug-Bau
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.1.texto: Paraphrase. "After the flood had swept over everything and kingship had descended from heaven, kingship was in Kish". Twenty-three kings follow, with reigns of 1,200 to 300 years. Among them: "Etana, the shepherd, who went up to heaven and consolidated all the foreign lands, became king; he ruled for 1,500 years". Then kingship passes to Eanna (Uruk): Meskiaggasher, son of Utu, who entered the sea and came out to the mountains; Enmerkar, who built Uruk; Lugalbanda the shepherd; Dumuzi the fisherman; and the divine Gilgamesh, whose father was a phantom (lil), lord of Kulaba, who ruled for 126 years; then his son Ur-Nungal, 30 years. Further on we read: "In Kish, Kug-Bau, the tavern keeper, who made firm the foundations of Kish, became king; she ruled for 100 years".
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.1.fuente: Paraphrase based on ETCSL 2.1.1 and Jacobsen (1939)
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.1.nota_acad: The list mixes historical figures (Enmebaragesi of Kish is attested in Early Dynastic inscriptions, c. 2600 BC) with legendary heroes. The short notes added to some names summarize legends: Etana and his flight, Meskiaggasher and the sea, Gilgamesh and his phantom father. Kug-Bau (Ku-Baba) is the only woman listed as king (lugal), not as queen consort; she was remembered as a former tavern keeper, and later tradition (the Weidner Chronicle) explains her rise by a favor to Marduk.
t.textos.lista-reyes.pasajes.1.lectura_a: Kug-Bau, a tavern keeper turned king, is an exceptional case in the male royal ideology of Mesopotamia; gender studies use her to show how official texts make female power both visible and marginal, associating it with popular trades and with transgression.
Zainab Bahrani, Women of Babylon: Gender and Representation in Mesopotamia, 2001
t.textos.anzu.version: Standard Babylonian version in 3 tablets (Neo-Assyrian copies from Nineveh, Assur and Sultantepe, 8th–7th centuries BC); there is a shorter Old Babylonian version (Susa), in which the hero is Ningirsu
t.textos.anzu.estructura.0.sinopsis: Proem in praise of Ninurta. Birth of Anzu, a monstrous bird (an eagle with a lion's head), on Mount Hehe. Enlil sets him as guardian of the entrance to his sanctuary. Seeing Enlil bathing without his insignia, Anzu steals the Tablet of Destinies from him and flees to the mountain; the order of the world is paralyzed. The gods look for a champion; Adad, Girra and Shara refuse.
t.textos.anzu.estructura.1.sinopsis: Ea proposes that the mother goddess (Belet-ili, Mami) send her son Ninurta. She agrees and gives him battle instructions. First encounter: Ninurta's arrows come apart because Anzu, with the Tablet, orders the reeds to return to their reed bed. Ninurta sends his weapon Sharur to consult Ea, who advises wearing Anzu out and cutting off his wings.
t.textos.anzu.estructura.2.sinopsis: Ninurta follows the advice, cuts off Anzu's feathers, pierces him with arrows and kills him. He recovers the Tablet of Destinies. The gods celebrate him and grant him temples and numerous names, in a final litany of exaltation.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. Anzu, stationed before the gate of Enlil's sanctuary, often gazes at the father of the gods, his crown of lordship, his divine garments and the Tablet of Destinies he holds in his hands. He conceives in his heart the desire to take away his power: "I will take the Tablet of Destinies of the gods and master the decrees of all the gods; I will occupy the throne and be lord of the rites". At dawn, while Enlil washes with pure water and leaves his crown on the throne, Anzu seizes the Tablet and flies to the mountain. Silence spreads, the rites cease, the radiance of the sanctuary fades. Enlil is struck dumb; the gods gather in bewilderment.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on Annus (2001) and Vogelzang (1988)
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.0.nota_academica: The Tablet of Destinies (ṭuppi šīmāti) is an object that guarantees the power to decree the order of the world; it also appears in the Enuma Elish (in Qingu's hands) and, in iconography, can be imagined as a seal or legal document of the divine assembly. Anzu (Sumerian Anzud) is a storm bird depicted with an eagle's body and a lion's head from the 3rd millennium (emblem of Ningirsu at Lagash, on Eannatum's "Stele of the Vultures"). In the Sumerian poem Lugalbanda and the Anzud Bird he appears as a favorable bird.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.0.lectura_astronau: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985), Sitchin turns the Tablet of Destinies into the control equipment of the Anunnaki "mission control center" at Nippur (the Duranki, "bond of heaven and earth"), and Anzu into a rebel astronaut who seizes it. The fight with Ninurta would be a duel between aircraft.

The poem presents a mythical fight with bow, arrows, winds and storms between a warrior god and a monstrous bird, with details from falconry (cutting the wings). Duranki is a poetic name for Nippur as a cosmic center. The Tablet functions as a symbol of legal and religious authority, just like seals in royal administration; nothing in the text describes a machine.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.ref: Tablets II–III (the fight and Ea's advice)
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.texto: Paraphrase. Ninurta gathers the seven winds of the storm, advances against the mountain, and Anzu challenges him: "I have stolen all the rites; who are you who come to fight with me?". Ninurta shoots, but Anzu shouts at the arrow: "Reed that approaches, go back to your reed bed; wood of the bow, go back to your forest; string, go back to the sheep; feathers, go back to the bird!". Thanks to the Tablet, his command is carried out and the arrows do not reach him. Ninurta sends Sharur, his mace, to tell Ea. Ea replies: fight without stopping until Anzu tires, make the wind tear the feathers from his wings and, when he cries to his feathers "wings to the wings!", shoot. Ninurta does so, cuts off his feathers, pierces his heart and kills him. The wind carries his feathers as news of the victory.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.fuente: Paraphrase based on Annus (2001) and Vogelzang (1988)
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.nota_academica: The scene shows the performative power of the word combined with the Tablet: Anzu undoes each arrow into its original materials. Ninurta's victory reproduces the scheme of the Enuma Elish (and perhaps served as its model): a young god, champion of the assembly, defeats the rebel and receives exaltation. A. Annus studied Ninurta's relationship with Assyrian royal ideology, in which the king is the warrior who restores order.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.lectura_actual.l: The myth is interpreted as an allegory of royal power: order depends on who possesses the symbols of authority, and their theft brings the world to a halt. The Assyrian kings, who presented themselves as Ninurta, used the story to legitimize their campaigns as the restoration of cosmic order.
t.textos.anzu.pasajes.1.lectura_actual.r: Amar Annus, The God Ninurta in the Mythology and Royal Ideology of Ancient Mesopotamia (SAAS 14), 2002
t.textos.etana.version: Akkadian poem known in three versions: Old Babylonian (Susa, c. 1800 BC), Middle Assyrian (Assur) and Standard Babylonian (Nineveh, 7th century BC, probably 4 tablets); the ending is lost
t.textos.etana.estructura.0.sinopsis: The gods found the city of Kish, but there is still no king; Ishtar looks for a shepherd and Enlil chooses Etana. Kingship descends from heaven. Etana is pious, but he has no son.
t.textos.etana.estructura.1.sinopsis: An eagle and a snake that live in a poplar beside the temple of Adad swear before Shamash to be allies and hunt together. The eagle breaks the pact and devours the snake's young. On Shamash's advice, the snake hides in the carcass of a wild bull, catches the eagle, cuts off its wings and throws it into a pit to die.
t.textos.etana.estructura.2.sinopsis: Etana asks Shamash for the "plant of birth". Shamash sends him to the pit, where Etana feeds and heals the eagle for months. In return, the eagle will carry him to Anu's heaven in search of the plant. Premonitory dreams of Etana and of his wife.
t.textos.etana.estructura.3.sinopsis: The flight: the eagle rises with Etana stage by stage and asks him to look at the earth, ever smaller. In one version Etana is afraid and they fall; in another they reach the gate of the gods. The ending has been lost, but the King List says that his son Balih succeeded him, which suggests a happy ending.
t.textos.etana.pasajes.0.ref: Tablet II (the eagle and the snake)
t.textos.etana.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. In the crown of a poplar the eagle nests; at its root, the snake. They swear before Shamash: "Whoever oversteps the bounds of Shamash, may Shamash hand him over to the executioner". For a time they hunt together and share the prey with their young. When the eagle's young grow up, it plans to devour the snake's young. A very wise eaglet warns it not to do so, because Shamash's net will catch it, but the eagle does not listen and devours them. The snake weeps before Shamash, who advises it to hide in the belly of a dead wild bull on the mountain, wait for the eagle to come down to eat and catch it. So it does: it seizes the eagle by the wings, plucks out its feathers and throws it into a pit to die of hunger and thirst.
t.textos.etana.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on Kinnier Wilson (1985) and Haul (2000)
t.textos.etana.pasajes.0.nota_academica: The story of the eagle and the snake is a fable about the oath and the justice of Shamash (god of the Sun and of justice) inserted into the royal story. The motif has been compared with later fables (Aesop, the Panchatantra). The "pit" is a trap on the mountain.
The animals speak, swear oaths and are subjects of justice before the Sun god: current readings stress that the fable does not separate humans and animals within the moral community, and that the broken pact between species precedes and makes possible Etana's human story.
Synthesis of readings from animal studies; see the introduction to Haul, Das Etana-Epos, 2000
t.textos.etana.pasajes.1.texto: Paraphrase. Every day Etana prays to Shamash and offers him lambs: "O Lord, let it come forth from your mouth: give me the plant of birth, show me the plant of birth, take away my shame and give me a son". Shamash answers him that he should go to the mountain and find the pit; inside there is an eagle that will show him the plant. Etana finds the eagle, which promises him whatever he wants if he gets it out of there. For seven or eight months Etana feeds it and teaches it to fly again, until it regains its strength.
t.textos.etana.pasajes.1.fuente: Paraphrase based on Kinnier Wilson (1985) and Dalley (1989)
t.textos.etana.pasajes.1.nota_academica: The lack of an heir is a dynastic threat, and the "plant of birth" (šammu ša alādi) recalls the remedies against infertility documented in medical and ritual texts. The rescue of the eagle joins the two threads of the story: the animal fable and the royal legend.
Etana's plea is read alongside the medical texts on infertility and childbirth: the "shame" of having no children is attributed here to the king, not to the woman, which contrasts with the tendency of the medical sources to locate the problem in the female body.
Synthesis; see Rivkah Harris, Gender and Aging in Mesopotamia, 2000
